title: Bharata and the deer
hookLine: a king who gave up a kingdom is undone by love for a fawn: raga and dvesha, the pull and the push
carry: raga and dvesha: the pull and the push
tomorrow: a king is told he has seven days to live. how does he spend them?
last: ASMITA: THE SEER MISTAKEN FOR WHAT IT SEES.

lines: A FAWN FALLS INTO THE RIVER.
HE SAVES IT. THEN HE KEEPS IT.
cards: King Bharata has done what kings almost never do. He's handed his kingdom to his sons and gone to live by a river as a hermit, to worship and meditate. One morning a pregnant doe comes to drink.
A lion roars nearby. She leaps the river in terror, her fawn drops into the water, and she dies on the far bank. The newborn is drowning.
Bharata wades in and saves it. That's kindness, and the Bhagavata Purana says so. Then he starts raising it.

teach.h: A FAWN SAVED. A HEART CAUGHT.
teach.b: He feeds the fawn, plays with it, panics when it wanders off. His prayers get shorter; his thoughts of the deer get longer. The man who let go of a kingdom can't let go of one small animal.

When Bharata dies, the deer is beside him, and his last thought is the deer. The story says he's born next as a deer, still remembering who he was. The Gita teaches the same: what you think of at the end, you go to.
Now Patanjali names what caught him. Sutra 2.7: attraction follows pleasure. Sutra 2.8: aversion follows pain.
Raga and dvesha. The key word is anushayi, resting upon: each rests on a memory.

teach.h: RAGA FOLLOWS PLEASURE. DVESHA FOLLOWS PAIN.
teach.b: Vyasa puts it plainly: raga is the thirst for pleasure in one who remembers pleasure; dvesha, the resentment of pain in one who remembers pain. In these sutras love isn't the problem, and neither is pleasure.
The affliction is the grip that grows, until a memory decides for you. And the two are partners: the deer's sweetness made every absence frightening.
The Gita names them as a pair: raga and dvesha sit in the senses; don't fall under their sway. Today it's the person, the show, the phone you reach for before you've chosen to.
Love it. Just notice when the pull has taken the wheel.

how: Bharata's story, from the fifth book of the Bhagavata Purana, is often told as a caution about attachment. Some Hindu teachers in yoga and Vedanta lineages ask students to watch raga and dvesha in daily life, pausing before acting on a like or dislike, and the Bhagavad Gita also names them as obstacles on the path.

o: resting upon: following after a memory
rising up out of nowhere, by chance

games.q: the hermit and the sutras — tap the pairs.

s: the Bhagavata says Bharata was wrong to save the fawn
saving it was kindness. the trouble was the grip that grew until it took his prayers and his last thought.
Vyasa ties attraction to the memory of pleasure
raga is thirst for pleasure in one who remembers pleasure.
Patanjali says pleasure itself is an affliction
the affliction is raga, the grip that follows the memory of pleasure.

games.q: Bharata gave up a whole kingdom, then got caught by a fawn. by sutra 2.7, what caught him?
o: raga: a pull resting on remembered sweetness, growing until it decided for him.
the deer was a demon in disguise.
dvesha: deep down he hated being a king.
games.why: attraction follows pleasure. the fawn was innocent and the rescue was right; the grip, resting on memory, is the affliction.

practice: Watch for tiny pulls and pushes as you sit: an itch you want to scratch, a thought of something nice later, a sound you wish would stop. Name each one gently, raga or dvesha, and wait one breath before doing anything.
If you pray, try it during your prayer and notice where the mind wanders off to. Often the pull fades by itself.

wordCard.voice: Anushayi, following after, resting upon. Raga, attraction, follows the memory of pleasure; dvesha, aversion, follows the memory of pain: grooves that pull and push the mind.

orig.note: Sanskrit rāga: attraction, passion; also 'color'. its mirror is dveṣa, aversion.

carryVoice: Your line: raga and dvesha, the pull and the push. Bharata's love was good; the grip was the trouble. That's day four hundred fifty-one.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 5.7–5.8 (King Bharata retires to the river; the doe and the lion; he raises the fawn; his last thought is the deer, and he is born a deer remembering his past)

Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 2.7–2.8 (thirst for pleasure in one who remembers pleasure)
Bhagavad Gita 3.34 (attraction and aversion in the senses)
Bhagavad Gita 8.6 (what one remembers at the end, one goes to)
